extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century literary essays / readers of Oliver Wendell Holmes
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective, humorous 19th‑century prose essay mixing anecdotes, moral observations, and advice to readers about imagination, manners, vice, and the creative life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat vices by finding and removing the 'head'
rubrics_metrics.description: Find where the 'head' of a vice lies and remove it carefully; do not merely break off a piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the Guinea-worm must be pulled out by the head with silk; breaking it leaves worse trouble. Anti-pattern: treating only surface symptoms (breaking the tail) leads to recurrence or worse consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue against vices by acknowledging, then refuting their attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lie that a vice has no attractions; let it 'make out its case' in temptation and then answer it with stronger, truthful counter-arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Ithuriel-toad image: exposing the true shape rather than fighting a false denial increases persuasive power. Anti-pattern: moralizing by denial or pretending the vice is unattractive—this is ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root causes of intemperance: empty or ill-regulated minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Intemperance most readily fastens on minds that are empty, ill-regulated, or debilitated; lack of ideas and self-discipline predisposes one to vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive guidance: filling the head with wholesome ideas and teaching self-government reduces susceptibility. Distinguish between willful vice and misfortune (e.g., hereditary propensity or poverty).

rubrics_metrics.name: On stimulants and creative persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative/reverie-based faculties are more vulnerable to imitation by artificial stimulants; reasoning faculties (voluntary effort) are safer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: poets and artists who operate in automatic/reverie states may be tempted to use alcohol/opium to rouse faculties when body or mind flags. Ideal: sound body and adequate nourishment would make creative persons temperate; stimulants provide temporary rousing but 'spoil the machine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Some forms of alcoholic exaltation have temporary virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: There are early stages of alcoholic exaltation that can quicken speech, rouse sympathy, and warm the spirit—moments that might seem improvements in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: these 'alcoholic virtues' do not endure ('don’t wash'); they are transient and the subsequent damage outweighs the momentary benefit. Use this admission to inform honest moral argument rather than denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader instruction: attend to asides (brackets)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author asks readers to pay particular attention to bracketed paragraphs, which are asides directed especially to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: bracketed passages may address the reader directly and contain intimate revelations or clarifications; treat them as a separate channel of commentary within the essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for poetic sensibility in a reader
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who can transform trivial recollections or 'little brown seeds' into imaginative significance qualifies as a poet (i.e., possessing the requisite poetic imagination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for creators/readers: poetic value depends partly on the reader’s imaginative participation; the author supplies seeds, the reader may transfigure them into a banquet of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social demeanor: the true gentleman's face
rubrics_metrics.description: A true gentleman's face is 'calm-eyed, firm-mouthed'; avoid the 'terrible smile' of self-consciousness and the 'meaningless blushing' that indicate underbreeding or awkward self-regard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: the 'terrible smile' signals self-consciousness and is contagious—worse than a scowling face. Tone: prescriptive etiquette about composure and the outward signs of breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiquette for looking at attractive women in public
rubrics_metrics.description: A man has the right to at least two distinct, respectful looks at a comely female face: one to recognize, a second if an unusual attraction is detected; prolonged or impertinent staring is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended boundary: second look is an 'appreciating homage' not a prolonged stare. The street is likened to a picture-gallery where seeing is permitted within modest limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to find original ideas ('ovarian eggs' of thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original, rudimentary ideas (the 'ovarian eggs' of future civilization) often reside in a few individuals as inchoate tendencies; to access them you must habitually converse with such persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for seekers of fresh truth: follow the arc of opinion over time to spot those in advance of it; fresh truth seldom enters books directly—seek out people with nascent ideas and engage them in talk to nurture their development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiographical/poetic material: small accidents mark individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Trivial, particular memories (a specific pail, mug, or moment) are what preserve a person's individuality in memory; such small details are seed-material for poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers/memoirists: cultivate and preserve the small, idiosyncratic particulars of experience rather than relying on grand universal statements; these details confer uniqueness.
